content: Sleeping sickness, also known as Human African trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic disease caused by protozoa of the species Trypanosoma brucei. These parasites are transmitted to humans and animals through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The disease is endemic to certain regions of sub-Saharan Africa, affecting approximately 36 countries and an estimated 60 million people. Currently, between 50,000 and 70,000 individuals are believed to be infected, although the number of cases has declined in recent years. It is suspected that many cases remain unreported. In 2008, approximately 48,000 deaths were attributed to this disease. Historically, there have been four major epidemics: one between 1896 and 1906, primarily in Uganda and the Congo Basin; two others in the 1920s and 1970s across several African countries; and a more recent outbreak in Uganda in 2008. The disease is caused by two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei: T. b. rhodesiense and T. b. gambiense. The more severe form of the disease is associated with T. b. rhodesiense. The symptoms of African trypanosomiasis occur in two distinct stages. The first stage, known as the hemolymphatic phase, is characterized by fever, headaches, joint pain, and itching. During this phase, the parasites invade the circulatory and lymphatic systems, often causing significant swelling of the lymph nodes, which can become markedly enlarged. If left untreated, the disease progresses, leading to more extensive damage, including anemia and dysfunction of the endocrine, cardiac, and renal systems. The second stage, referred to as the neurological phase, begins when the parasites cross the blood-brain barrier and invade the central nervous system. The term sleeping sickness is derived from the symptoms observed during this phase, which include confusion, impaired coordination, and disruptions in the sleep-wake cycle. Patients may experience extreme fatigue during the day, alternating with periods of manic activity, and insomnia at night. Without treatment, the disease is invariably fatal, with progressive neurological deterioration leading to coma and death. Damage sustained during the neurological phase may be irreversible. General symptoms of the disease include anxiety, drowsiness, fever, headache, excessive sleepiness, nighttime insomnia, mood changes, sweating, swollen lymph nodes throughout the body, a painful and swollen red nodule at the site of the tsetse fly bite, and an uncontrollable urge to sleep. The disease is transmitted primarily through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. Following the bite, a painful, red swelling often develops at the site. The infection then spreads through the bloodstream, causing episodes of fever, headache, sweating, and lymph node swelling. Once the infection reaches the central nervous system, it produces the characteristic symptoms of sleeping sickness. When the brain becomes involved, behavioral changes such as fear and mood swings may occur, along with fever, headache, and weakness. In some cases, myocarditis (inflammation of the heart) may develop. In addition to tsetse fly bites, the disease can be transmitted through other routes, including: Mother-to-child transmission, where the parasite crosses the placenta to infect the fetus. Accidental laboratory infections, such as through handling infected blood or organ transplantation, though these are rare. Blood transfusion. Sexual contact, which is considered a rare mode of transmission. Individuals at the highest risk of contracting sleeping sickness are those living in or traveling to regions of Africa where the disease is endemic and where tsetse flies are prevalent. The disease is extremely rare in the United States and is typically only seen in travelers returning from affected areas. The definitive diagnosis of sleeping sickness is made by identifying Trypanosoma parasites in patient samples through microscopic examination. Samples that may be used for diagnosis include fluid from the chancre (the bite site), lymph node aspirates, blood, bone marrow, and cerebrospinal fluid (during the neurological stage). Detection of trypanosome-specific antibodies can also aid in diagnosis, but these methods have variable sensitivity and specificity and are not reliable as standalone diagnostic tools. Additionally, seroconversion occurs only after the onset of clinical symptoms in T. b. rhodesiense infections, limiting its diagnostic utility. Most antibody and antigen tests cannot distinguish between current and past infections. However, specific IgM levels in cerebrospinal fluid may provide useful information. Other diagnostic methods include: Physical examination, which may reveal signs of meningoencephalitis (inflammation of the brain and meninges). Lymph node aspiration. It is critical to seek medical care promptly if symptoms of sleeping sickness develop. Early treatment is essential to prevent disease progression and fatal outcomes. Treatment for sleeping sickness depends on the stage of the disease and the subspecies of Trypanosoma involved. Medications used include: Eflornithine (effective only for T. b. gambiense infections). Melarsoprol. Pentamidine. Suramin (also known as Antrypol). b. gambiense but not T. b. rhodesiense. Insect control strategies, such as reducing tsetse fly populations, are also effective in preventing the spread of the disease in high-risk areas. Without treatment, sleeping sickness is fatal. Death may occur within six months due to cardiac failure or complications from T. b. rhodesiense infection. T. b. gambiense infections, which cause the classic sleeping sickness symptoms, progress more rapidly, often worsening over a few weeks. Both forms of the disease require immediate treatment to improve outcomes.
